nameStory: Coelastrum pulchrum gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'hollow star' and 'beautiful' - a fitting description for these microscopic algae that form stunning hollow spheres of interconnected cells. While it lacks a widely-used common name, scientists sometimes call it the 'beautiful star colony' for its distinctive geometric beauty.
description: This is a microscopic freshwater green alga that you'll never see with the naked eye, but becomes magical under a microscope. Individual colonies look like tiny hollow soccer balls made of 8-32 interconnected cells, each colony measuring only about 20-50 micrometers across (that's smaller than the width of a human hair!). The cells are arranged in a beautiful geometric pattern, connected by thin strands that give the whole colony a delicate, lace-like appearance. You'd need to collect pond water and examine it under magnification to discover these living jewels.

idTips.label: Colony Shape
idTips.description: Forms distinctive hollow spherical colonies that look like microscopic soccer balls or geodesic domes under magnification

idTips.label: Cell Arrangement
idTips.description: Individual cells are connected by thin cytoplasmic strands, creating gaps between cells that give the colony its characteristic openwork pattern

idTips.label: Colony Size
idTips.description: Each colony contains 8-32 cells and measures 20-50 micrometers across - invisible to the naked eye but clearly defined under a microscope

idTips.label: Cell Shape
idTips.description: Individual cells within the colony are roughly spherical to oval-shaped with bright green chloroplasts visible inside

idTips.label: Water Appearance
idTips.description: When abundant, may give pond water a slightly greenish tint, though individual colonies remain invisible without magnification

habitat: Found floating freely in the plankton of freshwater ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters and can be found in both natural water bodies and constructed ponds. Most commonly discovered in warmer, shallow areas where sunlight penetrates well, often associated with other microscopic algae and tiny aquatic creatures.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures rise and daylight increases. This is an excellent time to find them as spring runoff brings nutrients into water bodies.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when conditions are optimal for photosynthesis and reproduction. Colonies are most likely to be found during this season.
seasonality.fall: Populations may persist into early fall but begin to decline as temperatures drop and daylight decreases. Still possible to find in warmer water bodies.
seasonality.winter: Generally not active during winter months in New England, though some may survive in deeper waters or as dormant stages until spring returns.

funFact: Each tiny colony is actually a single organism made up of multiple cells that share resources through their connecting strands - like a microscopic city where every building is connected by bridges, and when one cell makes food through photosynthesis, it shares with its neighbors!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Coelastrum species, but can be distinguished by careful attention to colony size, cell number, and the specific pattern of cell connections. Other microscopic algae may form colonies, but few create the distinctive hollow sphere shape with connecting strands.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim flag**: This species is part of the fascinating world of phytoplankton - the 'grass of the water' that forms the base of aquatic food webs, though most people never realize these beautiful geometric forms exist in every pond they pass by.
compareHints: Compared to its close relatives like Coelastrum astroideum, C. pulchrum typically forms more regularly spherical colonies with more uniform cell spacing. Unlike C. microporum, which has very small pores between cells, C. pulchrum has more obvious gaps that give it its characteristic open, lacy appearance. **Uncertain claim flag**: The connecting strands between cells may be more prominent in C. pulchrum than in some other species in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Coelastrum astroideum differs from its relatives by having more pointed, pronounced cell projections than C.
